document_sections.heading: European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guideline on visual impairment in stroke
document_sections.content: This guideline addresses the diagnosis and management of visual impairment after ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke. It covers screening, specialist assessment and treatment across the stroke care pathway.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Visual impairment is frequent after stroke, but the best screening approach, screening time and management of different impairments remain disputed. The European Stroke Organisation (ESO) developed evidence-based guidance for clinicians caring for adult stroke survivors in prehospital services, stroke units, rehabilitation centres, eye departments and community services; survivors and caregivers are also intended readers. Development followed ESO procedures and GRADE: the group framed clinical questions, reviewed studies, conducted meta-analyses where possible, assessed evidence and issued recommendations or, when evidence was inadequate, expert consensus statements. Early screening within 1week of onset was found feasible and acceptable. The guideline examines screening accuracy before hospital arrival and during hyperacute and acute care, as well as specialist assessment. It suggests screening every patient with stroke to improve recognition of visual problems. Management covers central vision impairment, ocular stroke, eye movement disorders, visual field loss, visual neglect and visual perceptual disorders. More definitive randomised trials and diagnostic accuracy studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: Plain language summary
document_sections.content: Up to three quarters of stroke survivors experience visual problems; most, about 60%, are caused by stroke, while others usually reflect pre-existing eye conditions. Patients and clinical teams may not recognise that stroke has affected vision. Possible impairments involve eye movements, central or peripheral vision, attention to part of the visual environment, and processing of visual information such as colour or recognition. The optimal screening method, timing and management remain uncertain. The reviewed studies identify screening approaches usable within days of onset and treatment options that depend on the impairment; they also expose areas needing better research. The guideline recommends vision screening to improve detection, using a validated tool or specialist vision team, with early screening within 3–4days of onset. For treatment, it recommends visual scanning or visual search to support adaptation to field loss; thrombolysis within 4.5h of onset for ocular stroke; early measures such as glasses to improve acuity; referral for specialist management of eye movement disorders; and interventions tailored to visual neglect or perceptual deficits. It recommends collaboration among stroke teams, particularly occupational therapy, neuropsychology and eye care, alongside suitable information, resources and vision aids for survivors and caregivers.

document_sections.heading: Table of key recommendations/suggestions of the Vision Guideline
document_sections.content: The summary calls for screening all stroke survivors for visual problems, using a standardised, validated tool or specialist eye assessment and undertaking early screening within 3–4days of onset. It sets out compensatory visual scanning or search for field loss; thrombolysis for ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion) within 4.5h of onset if there are no contraindications; early measures to improve acuity; specialist eye referral for movement disorders; and individually targeted care for neglect or perceptual deficits. It also calls for cooperation among stroke, neuropsychology and eye care teams and provision of vision-related information, materials and aids to survivors and caregivers.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Post-stroke visual impairment can affect central and peripheral vision, eye movements, visual attention and visual perception. Reported prevalence is about 75% and incidence about 60% of stroke survivors. These problems are often missed, and care varies internationally without consistent diagnostic or management practices. Many international stroke guidelines omit them. Although screening and intervention research has grown, an up-to-date evidence overview was lacking. ESO commissioned this guidance for health professionals, researchers, policy makers, survivors and caregivers, concentrating on diagnosis and management. Its inclusive definition covers any visual-function problem following ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke. Questions used the Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcomes (PICOs) format without restricting topics to those likely to have high-quality trials. When evidence could not support a recommendation, the multidisciplinary group planned an expert opinion based on available information. Prespecified study criteria covered design, population size and follow-up; remaining research gaps informed proposed priorities for future work.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The guideline used ESO procedures and the GRADE framework to develop evidence-based recommendations and, where these were not possible, expert consensus statements.

document_sections.heading: Composition and approval of the Module Working Group
document_sections.content: ESO initiated the work. Fiona Rowe assembled and coordinated the Guideline Module Working Group, which ultimately comprised ten experts and two chairpersons, Fiona Rowe and Anne Hege Aamodt. Expertise included stroke medicine, neurology, neuropsychology, ophthalmology and orthoptics. Sex and geographical diversity were considered. The ESO Guideline Board and Executive Committee reviewed members’ disclosures and approved the group.

document_sections.heading: Development and approval of clinical questions
document_sections.content: Development followed ESO SOPs based on GRADE. The group selected clinically important topics and formulated PICO questions, reviewed by two external reviewers and ESO representatives, five reviewers in total. Group members rated candidate outcomes as critical, important or of limited importance. A closed Delphi vote used a 9-point scale, with 1–3 denoting ‘not important’ and 7–9 ‘critical’; critical outcomes were selected for each PICO and approved by the ESO Guidelines Board and Executive Committee.

document_sections.heading: Literature search
document_sections.content: The group and methodologist developed searches for each PICO, adapting validated strategies and updating relevant systematic reviews where appropriate. Relevant reviews were found for all PICOs. MEDLINE, Scopus, CINAHL and AMED were searched from previous review dates, earliest January 2011, through March 2023. Review reference lists, personal libraries, earlier guidelines and trial registries supplied additional records or information on ongoing work. In Covidence, two or more members independently screened titles and abstracts, then potentially eligible full texts; a third resolved disagreements. RCTs were prioritised, but registry analyses and large observational studies were considered when trial data were limited or an RCT design was unsuitable. Studies generally needed at least 20 adult (>18years) stroke patients; smaller studies were considered proof of concept unless formally powered. Human studies with mixed causes were eligible when >50% had stroke-related disease. Conference abstracts alone and non-English reports that the group could not translate were excluded. Recommendations cover hyperacute, acute, subacute and chronic presentation and follow-up. Vision screening means checklists or more detailed standardised forms or tools administered by any stroke-team member; specialist assessment means evaluation by an eye-care professional or a neuropsychologist, particularly for persistent neglect or perceptual disorders.

document_sections.heading: Data analysis
document_sections.content: The working group extracted and analysed data and contacted study authors about unreported eligible results; unanswered requests left the data missing. Effects were reported with 95% confidence intervals (95%CIs). The methods also specify calculations for combining group means and for combining standard deviations when group sizes differ.

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the quality of evidence and formulation of recommendations
document_sections.content: For each PICO outcome, appraisal considered study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and other biases. RCTs were assessed with the Cochrane tool. Rather than calculate a discouraged overall quality score, assessors judged bias for individual studies and used GRADEpro to assign final evidence ratings of high, moderate, low or very low. Diagnostic-accuracy synthesis used QUADAS-2 for bias and applicability, alongside inspection of forest plots for consistency and consideration of estimate precision. Subgroups discussed GRADE and QUADAS assessments with the whole working group. Recommendation wording required full agreement after Delphi voting; direction and strength followed GRADE evidence profiles and ESO procedures.

document_sections.heading: Basis for recommendations:
document_sections.content: The grading table relates recommendation wording to the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences. Strong recommendations favouring or opposing an intervention indicate that one side clearly outweighs the other in most settings; weak recommendations indicate a probable advantage or uncertainty. Ungraded consensus-based statements indicate probable benefit despite little evidence. The working group added expert consensus statements when evidence-based recommendations were not possible but clinical guidance was needed. These statements reflect group opinion reached by Delphi voting and must not be treated as evidence-based recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Drafting of the document, revision and approval
document_sections.content: Each PICO section presents an analysis of current evidence, adds relevant subgroup, ongoing-study or other clinical information when needed, and then gives a recommendation or expert consensus statement according to the evidence. All group members reviewed successive drafts until agreeing on the complete guideline. The final submission underwent external and ESO review.

document_sections.heading: Results DIAGNOSIS
document_sections.content: The diagnostic questions assess whether screening or specialist evaluation identifies visual impairment and specific visual deficits, and whether earlier recognition improves activities or quality of daily life.

document_sections.heading: PICO 1: For adults with visual problems due to stroke, does routine use of vision screening, compared to no routine vision screening, improve detection rate?
document_sections.content: This question compares routine vision screening with its absence for detecting stroke-related visual problems at any stage, with particular interest in hyperacute and acute care.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: Upwards of 40% of survivors with confirmed visual impairment do not or cannot report symptoms, so symptom reports alone cannot establish whether impairment is present. Eight studies compared vision tools or tests with no routine vision screening or other stroke screens; their median sample size was 100 (range 43–736; mean 204.1, SD 236.4). Designs included diagnostic-accuracy, cohort and cross-sectional studies, with no RCTs; only two directly compared against no routine screening. Prehospital studies examined BEFAST against FAST and V-FAST against NIHSS. Six hospital studies examined CVSQ, applications including VISA, StrokeVision and MRFn, and paper-based VISA or SVDST. Sensitivity and specificity were available for seven studies. Most studies had high bias risk associated principally with non-RCT designs, although QUADAS assessment generally indicated low risk; heterogeneity, unblinded result interpretation and incomplete reporting of missing data limited confidence. Table 1.1 summarises diagnostic accuracy and QUADAS-2 findings; Figure 1.1 shows bias domains and Figure 1.2 shows accuracy forest plots. VFAST sensitivity and specificity were 85 and 42%, respectively; averages for hospital tools were 87.3% and 81.8%. Fourteen studies reported detection rates, with median sample size 73.5 (range 23–88,664; mean 6596.5, SD 23,623.6). Across stages from prehospital to chronic stroke, mean detection was 64.6% (SD 28.8; median 70.5%, range 11.7–96.5%). Differences reflected study design, recruitment and the impairments assessed.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Sensitivity, specificity and detection rate were the prioritised outcomes; false results, predictive values and assessment units were not included despite their relevance. Early testing is unlikely to take long or entail risk, and patients are likely to accept it. Compared with no screening, screening better detects impairment and may reduce diagnostic delay or error, with consequences for rehabilitation and sometimes treatment or survival. Where a positive screen prompts further evaluation, sensitivity may take priority over specificity despite additional testing for some people. Available formal checklists and tools include BEFAST and V-FAST before hospital arrival, and CVSQ, MRFn, SVDST and VISA for inpatient or community use. They consistently identify more problems than no visual screen, especially in hospital. Rapid adjuncts to FAST suit prehospital and emergency decisions but emphasise stroke detection, particularly posterior circulation stroke, and can miss visual deficits. More detailed tools take longer but provide more precise detection; specialist examinations may increase detection further. Identifying posterior circulation stroke without other neurological signs, or ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion) within 4h of onset, can allow timely thrombolysis. The tools were feasible from prehospital care to acute stroke units, and screening was acceptable to staff and patients, often within 3days of onset. At least 40% of affected survivors do not or cannot describe symptoms. The evidence-based recommendation suggests screening adults with stroke with a validated tool or specialist eye-team assessment to improve detection; specialist assessment increases accuracy beyond screening. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: PICO 2: For adults with visual problems due to stroke, does early assessment within one week of stroke admission, compared to later assessment, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: This question concerns whether screening or assessment within 1week of stroke onset, rather than later, improves daily activities and quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: No study directly compared early with later vision screening or assessment for this question.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Four relevant but indirectly applicable studies comprised two cohorts, one cross-sectional study and one online questionnaire. The three patient studies had median sample size 349 (range 245–1295; mean 629.7, SD 578.5); the median number screened was 245 (range 22–1033; mean 433.3, SD 531.2). Hospital stay and time to visual testing were prioritised. Across two studies, mean hospital stay for visually impaired survivors was 49.69days (SD 67.84); one reported 13.5days (SD 45.9) for survivors with normal vision. Stay was significantly longer with impairment, but greater stroke severity was also significantly associated with stay, precluding a causal interpretation or a conclusion that earlier vision testing shortens admission. Early assessment might help predict discharge, but this requires study. One study assessed over 70% within 4days: median initial screening time was 3days (IQR 2), and median specialist-assessment time was 4days (IQR 7). Norup et al. reported referral of 81.8% to a vision team at a mean of 8days (SD 8.30) after admission. In a practice survey, 35.5% of orthoptists saw patients within 2weeks and 55.5% by 1month; usual overall vision-care follow-up was less than 3months. In Räty et al.’s study of occipital stroke with isolated visual symptoms, only 20.8% reached hospital within the 4.5h thrombolysis window. Failure to recognise symptoms or delays during other specialist evaluations contributed to missed treatment opportunities, supporting prompt stroke-unit referral. Assessment within 1week is feasible and acceptable for most patients, takes little time and has no reported side effects. Recognition may bring forward patching, prisms or scanning rehabilitation and inform other therapies, but a benefit of early versus later assessment for daily activities or quality of life was not demonstrated. Survivors may be unaware of deficits or unable to report them. Because recovery cannot be predicted and only a small percentage recover early within 3–4weeks of onset, delaying everyone’s assessment may restrict adaptation and rehabilitation for those with persistent impairment. The studies were mostly non-RCTs at high risk of bias, heterogeneous and limited by unblinded interpretation and incomplete reporting; meta-analysis was not possible. Table 2.1 reports timing, hospital stay and GRADE findings, and Figure 2 presents bias assessment. Visually impaired survivors had significantly poorer Barthel Index and EQ-5D-5L outcomes, particularly for mobility and usual activities, but studies did not test improvement attributable to earlier assessment. Evidence was insufficient for an evidence-based recommendation on early screening. Quality of evidence: Low ⊕⊕. Strength of recommendation: not assessable (–). By consensus, 10 of 10 experts suggest screening early to identify visual problems, feasibly within 3–4days of onset, with most patients assessable within 1-week; a specialist eye team or at least a validated screening tool should be used.

document_sections.heading: PICO 3: For adults with visual field loss due to stroke, does identification of visual field loss by vision screening or specialist eye team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life?
document_sections.content: The question compares visual-field identification through dedicated screening or eye-team assessment with routine stroke screening, considering detection, daily activities and quality of life at any stroke stage.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: No study directly compared objective visual-field outcomes from dedicated screening or specialist assessment against routine stroke screening.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Nineteen relevant studies were indirect: they evaluated visual symptoms rather than objective fields, or compared vision screening with specialist assessment rather than routine stroke screening. Four comparative tool studies had median sample size 101 (range 48–883; mean 249.6, SD 355.0) and median number screened 101 (range 45–883; mean 246.8, SD 356.5). They studied StrokeVision App, VISA in print or app form, and PreHAST. Across all four, sensitivity ranged from 5.3 to 92.9%; PreHAST sensitivity was 5.3%. After admission, tool sensitivity against standard confrontation ranged from 71.0% to 92.9% (average 82.8%) and specificity from 70.9% to 89.7% (average 82.2%). Most studies had low QUADAS bias risk. Table 3.1 summarises accuracy and QUADAS-2 findings; Figures 3.1 and 3.2 present bias domains and accuracy plots. Fifteen studies of field-defect detection had median sample size 170 (range 22–1204; mean 302.8, SD 357.5). Detection ranged from 18.1% to 79.0% (mean 40.4, SD 21.1, median 27.9), varying with field indices, testing methods and stroke populations. Ten studies used specialist assessment and five screening. Formal perimetry, confrontation, tangent screens, Amsler grid and applications were among the methods used. Homonymous hemianopia was the most frequent field defect. App-based tests were reported acceptable. Rowe et al. found 79.8% could undergo assessment within 1week; pooled analysis found assessment within the first month in 90% of cases, with median timing 3days. Screening and specialist assessment took a reasonable time and had no associated risks. Prompt testing matters because field loss can be the sole presentation of posterior cerebral artery stroke: an estimated 90% of occipital infarcts have only visual sequelae, and 46% of survivors with field loss report no visual symptoms. Monocular versus binocular loss should be distinguished. Suspected ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion) needs rapid ophthalmic referral. An early fundus examination may not yet show ischaemia despite possible later cherry-red-spot findings; optical coherence tomography can identify inner retinal nerve layer hyper-reflectivity, and telemedicine may accelerate confirmation. Delayed stroke recognition can affect rehabilitation, quality of life and, in some cases, survival. Evidence has not established that identifying field loss through dedicated screening or specialist assessment rather than routine stroke screening improves daily activities or quality of life. Data were insufficient for an evidence-based recommendation on that comparison. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: not assessable (–). By consensus, 10 of 10 experts suggest early field-loss screening, feasible within 3–4days and achievable for most within 1week, using specialist assessment or at least a validated tool. They state that dedicated screening improves detection relative to routine stroke screening and specialist assessment further improves diagnostic accuracy.

document_sections.heading: PICO 4: For adults with central vision impairment due to stroke, does identification of visual acuity loss by vision screening or specialist eye team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life?
document_sections.content: This question examines whether dedicated visual-acuity screening or specialist eye assessment improves recognition and patient outcomes compared with routine stroke screening.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of the current evidence
document_sections.content: No study directly compared visual-acuity outcomes from dedicated screening or specialist assessment with routine stroke screening.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Eight relevant studies instead described acuity-related symptoms or compared dedicated screening with specialist assessment. Three comparative studies evaluated VISA and CVSQ, with median sample size 108.5 (range 100–461; mean194.5, SD 177.8) and median number screened 100.5 (range 89– 461; mean 187.7, SD 182.2). For the symptom-based CVSQ, sensitivity and specificity were 83.9% and 79.1% for reading problems and 74.7% and 86.7% for blurred vision. For objective VISA variants, averaged sensitivity and specificity were 62.3% and 81.0% for near acuity and 82.7% and 87.9% for distance acuity. Table 4.1 reports diagnostic accuracy and QUADAS-2 findings, while Figures 4.1 and 4.2 depict bias domains and accuracy. Six detection studies had median sample size 273 (range 23–1204; mean 455.2, SD 503.2); mean detection of acuity loss was 36.4% (SD 12.8; median 37.7%, range 20.9–54.0%), varying with design and population. Most had low QUADAS bias risk. Objective acuity measurement under good lighting promotes more consistent results. Central impairment mainly concerns acuity, measurable with charts or reading text of specified size; contrast sensitivity or colour vision can contribute in a minority of cases. Early identification could support referral and management, but the included studies did not specifically report the effect of impaired acuity on daily activities or quality of life. In one report, 58.5% of survivors with central impairment did not or could not report visual symptoms. Acuity testing was feasible and acceptable, often within 3days. Reduced acuity can reflect stroke, pre-existing ocular pathology or refractive error, or both; coexisting pathology was reported in about 30%, with childhood strabismus/amblyopia in a further 5.4%. Assessing acuity matters for safe mobility, reading and rehabilitation regardless of onset. No study established that dedicated identification, compared with routine stroke screening, improves detection together with daily activities or quality of life. Data were insufficient for an evidence-based recommendation on this comparison. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: Not assessable (–). By consensus, 10 of 10 experts suggest screening early for central impairment, feasibly within 3–4days and for most within 1week, through specialist assessment or at least a validated tool. They state that dedicated screening improves detection and specialist assessment further improves accuracy.

document_sections.heading: PICO 5: For adults with eye movement disorders due to stroke, does identification of strabismus and/or ocular motility deficit loss by vision screening or specialist eye team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life?
document_sections.content: The question examines identification of eye movement disorders by a vision screen or specialist eye assessment, relative to routine stroke screening.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: No study directly compared eye movement disorder outcomes from dedicated vision screening or specialist assessment against routine stroke screening.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Ten relevant studies reported dedicated screening or specialist assessment without the required routine-screen comparison. Three diagnostic-accuracy studies of VISA or V-FAST had median sample size 101 (range 43–116, mean 86.7, SD 38.5) and median number screened 89 (range 43–89; mean 77.7, SD 30.6). Two related VISA studies provided sensitivity and specificity; pooling was inappropriate. Pilot VISA sensitivity was 16% and specificity 93.4%; after refinement, sensitivity was 66.7% and specificity 73.2%. Table 5.1 reports accuracy and QUADAS-2 assessment; Figures 5.1 and 5.2 show bias domains and accuracy plots. Eight reports on disorder detection had median sample size 46.5 (range 22–1204; mean 292.0, SD 480.1). Across prehospital through chronic stages, mean detection was 51.3% (SD 20.3; median 53.1%, range 27.2–78.0%); recruitment and study-design differences contributed to variation. Screening was feasible and acceptable, including acute testing often within 3days, but specialist orthoptic assessment was most accurate. A report found that 51.4% of affected survivors did not or could not report visual symptoms, supporting objective evaluation. Disorders can cause diplopia, blurred vision or oscillopsia; assessing their range requires examination of smooth pursuits, saccades, optokinetic nystagmus, vestibulo-ocular reflex and vergence. Evidence was insufficient to recommend an approach on the direct comparison with routine stroke screening. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: Not assessable (–). By consensus, 10 of 10 experts suggest early screening for movement disorders, feasible within 3–4days and for most within 1week, by a specialist eye team or at least a validated tool. They state that dedicated screening detects more disorders than routine stroke screening and specialist assessment improves accuracy further.

document_sections.heading: PICO 6: For adults with visual perceptual disorders due to stroke, does identification of visual perceptual disorders by screening proforma/tool or specialist team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life?
document_sections.content: This question addresses higher-order visual-processing impairments that prevent or hinder recognition by sight, considered separately from visual neglect.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: The planned comparison considered dedicated forms, questionnaires, test collections or specialist assessment against routine stroke screening, across care stages and particularly during acute care.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: In a 2019 survey of occupational therapists and orthoptists in the United Kingdom and Republic of Ireland, 93% reported observing function, 94% asking about symptoms, and only 18% using a specific screening test for perceptual disorders other than visual inattention. Seven other studies addressed symptoms or specialist vision outcomes without a routine-screen comparator. Only one reported CVSQ sensitivity and specificity. All seven reported detection, with median sample size 220 (range 50–1500; mean 503.3, SD 524.2) and median number screened 220 (range 50 to 1,204; mean 461, SD 434.7). Table 6.1 presents accuracy and QUADAS-2 findings, and Figure 6.1 presents bias domains. Heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis. Mean detection was 11.2% across five general-stroke studies and 56.9% across two selected-subpopulation studies. Specialist-assessment studies yielded pooled prevalence 5.5% (95%CI: 4.8–6.2). Other methods reported 50.8% at 3weeks after returning home (35.9% at 6months) and 63%, respectively. Studies also assessed individual perceptual deficits without measuring overall disorder detection. Because none used routine stroke screening to obtain its detection rate, the added detection attributable to specialist assessment or a dedicated tool is unknown. Screening was feasible and acceptable, often within 3days, but specialist assessment using specific perceptual tests was more accurate than symptom questionnaires. Asking about symptoms alone may miss problems: about one-fifth of affected survivors do not report visual symptoms. Early recognition can permit reassurance about frightening or disabling experiences, including formed hallucinations and difficulty recognising familiar people or objects. No study established that dedicated screening improves activities or quality of life compared with routine stroke screening. Evidence was insufficient for an evidence-based recommendation on the comparison. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: Not assessable (–). By consensus, 10 of 10 experts suggest early screening, feasible within 3–4days and for most within 1week, by specialist assessment or at least a validated tool. They state that dedicated screening improves detection over routine screening and specialist assessment improves accuracy further.

document_sections.heading: PICO 7: For adults with visual neglect due to stroke, does identification of visual neglect by screening proforma/tool or specialist team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life?
document_sections.content: This question examines recognition of visual neglect or inattention regardless of subtype, including egocentric, allocentric, personal, peri-personal and extra-personal presentations.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: Sensitivity, specificity and detection rate were prioritised. Four studies comparing neglect assessment with routine stroke screening had median sample size 125.5 (range 67 to 428; mean 186.5, SD 163.6). Larger studies generally showed sensitivity of 83–91% with specificity of 32–94%, but restricted populations and different assessment methods limit generalisation. OCS had the lowest reported sensitivity, 52%, and driving performance the lowest specificity, 32%. Table 7.1 and Figures 7.1 and 7.2 present diagnostic-accuracy findings, QUADAS-2 assessment and forest plots.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Five further studies compared screening against other non-routine or specialist assessments. Their median sample size was 89 (range 44–116; mean 85.6, SD 25.6), and the mean number screened was 81.2 (SD 21.2; median 83.5, range 44–101). Across measures, sensitivity ranged from 60–95% and specificity from 61–94%. Thirteen detection studies had a median of 107 visually assessed participants (range 22– 1204; mean 303.9, SD 376.8); mean detection was 40%, SD 23.5 (median 33.2%, range 11.7–86.2%). Testing approach, hemisphere affected and time since stroke contributed to variation. Routine stroke screens typically used checklists or NIHSS; dedicated measures included paper tasks, Catherine Bergego scale, MAC, OCS, video-oculography, rapid unilateral neglect screening and VISA. MAC and video-oculography are valid assessment alternatives, but available evidence does not establish a substantial practical or diagnostic-accuracy advance over conventional paper tests in acute care. Some 58.4% of survivors with visual neglect reported no visual symptoms; anosognosia, communication problems or confusion may contribute. Missed neglect threatens functional independence. The guideline recommends early screening with a battery of tests because a single checklist or NIHSS observation lacks sensitivity. Dedicated screening and specialist assessment detect more neglect than routine screening, with more detailed approaches generally improving accuracy; everyday neglect can persist despite normal results on common tasks, so more demanding, ecologically valid tasks may improve sensitivity. Screening is acceptable and often possible within 3days. No study established that identifying neglect by dedicated screening improves daily activities or quality of life compared with routine stroke screening. The evidence-based recommendation suggests vision screening to improve neglect detection, with specialist assessment and a test battery for greater accuracy. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 High risk of bias. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: TREATMENT
document_sections.content: The treatment questions examine compensatory, substitutive and restitutive approaches for distinct post-stroke visual impairments.

document_sections.heading: PICO 8: For adults with homonymous visual field loss due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: For this question, compensatory treatment supports adaptation, substitutive treatment uses a device or optical aid to address impairment, and restitutive treatment aims to restore the visual field. Outcomes of interest included visual-field change, activities of daily living, quality of life, driving, reading and falls.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of the current evidence
document_sections.content: Nine RCTs compared interventions for post-stroke field loss, with mean sample size 44.6 (SD 19.5; median 45, range 24–87). Four assessed compensatory scanning or search training. Daily-activity improvement was significant in one trial but not another using different measures; vision-related VFQ-25 quality-of-life improvement was significant in three trials, whereas findings using EQ-5D or Beck depression inventory were not significant. In Rowe et al.’s trial, monocular prism segments produced non-significant changes in daily activities, quality of life and reading, with a 69% adverse-event rate. Five trials investigated perceptual or discrimination training, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, or transcranial alternating-current and direct-current stimulation. Two reported significant changes in mean visual-field deviation, but changes up to 3dB had limited clinical significance. VFQ-25 and reading findings differed between trials. Table 8.1 presents treatment outcomes and GRADE assessments, and Figure 8 presents bias assessment. Differences in intervention, outcomes and timing prevented meta-analysis. Most studies had high risk of bias, with heterogeneity, unblinded result interpretation and incomplete reporting of missing data.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Three additional cohort or cross-sectional studies addressed homonymous field-loss interventions; median sample size was 294 (range 22–426; mean 247.7, SD 205.5). Compensation aims to improve eye movements and searching toward the blind hemifield. Substitution, such as prisms, shifts otherwise unseen images into the sighted field. Restitution proposes improved visual-pathway function and possibly field area or sensitivity. Current evidence suggests compensatory scanning or search training has a positive, significant effect on daily activities, consistent with earlier systematic reviews. Training can begin as early as day 1 after onset but is usually started when the survivor can participate. Improvements in searching and daily activities or quality of life may occur without objective field recovery. Different scanning strategies may suit environmental exploration and reading. Evidence is insufficient that substitutive or restitutive training substantially changes the lost field area, and adverse events are possible. Further study is needed on sensitivity or discrimination within the affected area, intervention effectiveness, falls and driving; the reviewed studies reported no effects on falls or driving. The evidence-based recommendation suggests visual scanning or visual search to support adaptation and recommends starting treatment early when feasible and acceptable to the patient. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: Table 8.1. PICO 8 – For adults with homonymous visual field loss due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: The table compares compensatory scanning or search training, substitutive Fresnel prisms and restitutive approaches with control, sham or standard care across acute-to-chronic settings. It presents visual-field, daily-activity, quality-of-life and reading outcomes, adverse events and GRADE ratings. For compensatory training it records reports of headaches and fatigue; for monocular prisms it records headaches, diplopia, navigation difficulties, dizziness, optical glare and visual confusion. Its driving and falls outcomes are reported as unavailable. The restitutive portion presents study-specific field, cortical, daily-activity, quality-of-life and reading findings; comparisons vary by intervention, group and follow-up time.

document_sections.heading: PICO 8: For adults with homonymous visual field loss due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: Table 8.1 presents outcomes and GRADE assessments for compensatory, substitutive and restitutive approaches; Figure 8 presents study-level risk-of-bias assessments. The intervention studies varied in treatment, outcome measurement and timing, and most had a high risk of bias. Their heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Visual scanning/search training can improve compensatory adaptation to field loss in both early and chronic stroke. Improvements in scanning and search performance may help explain gains in daily activities and quality of life even when measured visual-field parameters do not improve. Different activities may require different scanning strategies, including strategies for environmental exploration and for reading. Evidence is insufficient to establish that substitutive or restitutive training substantially reduces the area of field loss; adverse events are possible. Further research should test whether these approaches improve sensitivity or discrimination within the affected field despite persistent static loss. Effects on falls and driving were not reported. More comprehensive studies of hemianopia interventions, particularly scanning/search training, are needed. The guideline notes ongoing trials involving a 3D game for eye-movement training, reading training and the SEARCH trial.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: For adults with post-stroke visual field loss, the guideline suggests compensatory visual scanning/visual search to support adaptation. It recommends starting treatment early, when feasible and acceptable to the patient. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: PICO 9: For adults with ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion), does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: This question concerns ocular stroke, also called central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), eye stroke or retinal stroke, across the stroke-care pathway, with particular interest in hyperacute treatment. Compensatory care helps adaptation, such as eccentric viewing; substitutive care uses an aid, such as spectacles or a magnifier; restitutive care seeks to restore visual function, such as through thrombolysis.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: The critical outcomes were visual-acuity change, quality of life and daily activities. Five comparative studies evaluated ocular-stroke interventions; mean sample size was 73.6 (SD 47.5; median 60; range 25–134). All were case-comparison or cohort studies rather than RCTs. Four assessed intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA/alteplase), and one assessed hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Limited evidence suggests that either treatment may benefit some survivors. No RCT was published during 2011-2023. Four studies reported visual-acuity change, two reported functional-activity change, and none reported quality of life. The activity findings indicate potential improvement in independence alongside vision after thrombolysis. Adverse events were also examined. Table 9.1 sets out visual-acuity and other outcomes with GRADE assessments; Figure 9 shows risk of bias. The studies had high risk of bias, heterogeneous methods, concerns about blinding and incomplete-data reporting, so meta-analysis was not possible.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: A further cohort study without a comparator evaluated intravenous liposomal prostaglandin E1 for acute CRAO. Studies of reperfusion, particularly rtPA (alteplase) within 4.5h, consistently reported visual-acuity improvement; significant gains of 0.7–1.0 logMAR were reported after rtPA/alteplase within 4.5h, whereas treatment after that window produced less improvement. Benefit may vary with event and patient characteristics. Although rtPA/alteplase for CRAO has been reported as feasible, safe and associated with better visual function than no treatment, RCT data for intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5h are lacking. Trials of alteplase or tenecteplase—THEIA, TenCRAOS and REVISION—are ongoing. Reported daily-activity differences between intervention and control groups suggest potential functional benefit and support considering thrombolysis for eligible patients, while weighing risks and individual preferences. Most survivors may accept treatment because of concern about sight loss; a small subset, particularly people relying on one unaffected eye, may decline it. Reported adverse events include intracerebral hemorrhage (1%), orolingual angioedema and systemic bleeding (up to 11%); these risks matter during consent discussions. CRAO is followed by increased short-term cerebral-stroke risk, warranting referral for cerebrovascular investigation as with transient ischemic attack or minor stroke. Care requires collaboration among family/general practitioners, primary eye care, ophthalmology and stroke physicians or neurologists.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: For adults with ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion), the guideline suggests thrombolysis within 4.5h of onset to assist visual-function recovery. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: PICO 10: For adults with central vision impairment due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: This question covers central visual impairment after stroke but excludes central retinal artery occlusion, addressed in PICO 9. Compensatory approaches aid adaptation, such as eccentric viewing; substitutive approaches use spectacles, magnifiers or other aids; restitutive approaches seek to restore visual function. Every stage of stroke care was considered.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of the current evidence
document_sections.content: No randomised controlled trial compared treatment of central visual impairment with no intervention, sham treatment or placebo.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: The critical outcomes were visual acuity and quality of life. Three observational cohort studies reported visual-acuity changes after intervention. Median sample size was 273 (range 77–1500; mean 616.7, SD 771.2), and the median number visually assessed was 77 (range 55–1204; mean 445.3, SD 657.1). None reported daily-activity or quality-of-life outcomes. Table 10.1 presents visual-acuity findings and GRADE assessment; Figure 10 presents risk of bias. Heterogeneity in interventions, measures and timing precluded meta-analysis. Most studies had high risk of bias, with unblinded interpretation and limited reporting on missing or complete data. In Freeman and Rudge's prospective stroke-unit cohort, 24 (44%) of 55 tested survivors had impaired acuity; 50% (n =12) improved over an average 63days (range 1week to 6months). Five received new or updated spectacles, while improvement in the others was spontaneous. Lotery et al. prospectively assessed 77 rehabilitation-unit survivors within 2weeks of admission: 26% (n =20) had acuity worse than 0.3 logMAR, and half improved after receiving new or updated glasses (n =10). In Rowe et al.'s prospective study of 1500 consecutive admissions, 1204 underwent visual assessment. From first to last visit, mean binocular near-acuity change was 0.33 logMAR and mean binocular distance-acuity change was 0.19 logMAR. Full recovery occurred in 35.6%, partial recovery in 36.4% and no improvement in 25.4%, over mean follow-up of 93.75days (SD 102.84): median 58days (range 1–530). Care included referral to optometry or low-vision services for 51.7%, and compensatory strategies or information for 25.4%. Reduced acuity may result from stroke, pre-existing ocular disease or refractive error, or both. Freeman and Rudge and Lotery et al. did not distinguish new from pre-existing impairment; Rowe et al. did. Co-existing ocular pathology affected about 30%, with childhood strabismus/amblyopia contributing a further 5.4%. Rowe et al. reported new stroke-related central impairment in 29.4% (n =354 stroke survivors). Improving acuity matters for safe mobility and participation in rehabilitation regardless of when the deficit arose. Evidence of improvement over time is limited and includes spontaneous recovery as well as effects of spectacles; studies differed in interventions and did not always identify the specific treatment. Robust studies should examine acuity, daily activities and quality of life. Evidence on age-related visual problems in the general population, addressed in other Cochrane reviews, remains relevant to individual treatment decisions. Survivors are likely to prefer acuity-improving care over none. Clinicians should offer information on reading and electronic aids, filters, environmental changes and other resources. Survivors should have access to their existing spectacles or be retested when these are lost, broken or old. Magnifiers may help if corrected central vision remains reduced; persistent reduction warrants optometry and ophthalmology evaluation.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient for an evidence-based recommendation for or against compensatory, substitutive or restitutive interventions for adults with post-stroke central visual impairment. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Not assessable (–).

document_sections.heading: Expert consensus statement
document_sections.content: 10 of 10 experts suggest offering acuity-improving management as soon as possible after stroke. Survivors should use prescribed spectacles, have lost, broken or outdated spectacles replaced or updated promptly, and receive directions to suitable information, resources and vision aids.

document_sections.heading: PICO 11: For adults with eye movement disorders due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: The question considers treatment of post-stroke eye-movement disorders throughout care. Compensatory approaches support adaptation, such as eye-scanning training; substitutive approaches use devices or optical aids, such as prism or occlusion; restitutive approaches seek to restore alignment and motility, such as extraocular muscle surgery.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: Critical outcomes were eye-movement range, daily activities and quality of life. Two comparative studies of compensatory interventions were identified: one RCT and one observational case-control study. Mean sample size was 76.5 (SD 17.7; median 76.5, range 64–89). One included stroke-related ocular-motility disturbance generally; the other addressed binocular dysfunction. Table 11.1 reports intervention outcomes and GRADE assessments, and Figure 11 reports risk of bias. Differences in intervention, measurement and treatment timing prevented meta-analysis. The studies were described as having high risk of bias, including concerns about heterogeneity, unblinded interpretation and incomplete-data reporting.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Three further single-group cohorts assessed compensatory or substitutive care. Their median sample size was 30 (range 20–1500; mean 516.7, SD 851.6), and the median visually assessed was 30 (range 20–1204; mean 418, SD 680.7). One covered any stroke-related ocular-motility disturbance and two covered binocular dysfunction. Training combining clinician-led and home exercises produced significant improvements in binocular functions, daily activities and quality of life, but a stroke-specific treatment effect could not be determined across the diverse disorders. This uncertainty does not establish ineffectiveness. Research in similar disorders after other acquired brain injuries supports interventions including prisms, botulinum toxin and extraocular muscle surgery. Prisms have long-standing accepted use for correcting binocular diplopia, with established clinical and cost effectiveness; the guideline states that further research evaluation of these established uses is unnecessary. When a prism is unsuitable for early diplopia relief, a patch or other occlusion is recommended. Prism or occlusion is usually applied to the affected eye unless patient preference, including strong ocular dominance, favours otherwise. Occlusion may cover all or part of a spectacle lens; Blenderm, Micropore and Bangerter tape/foils can provide varying degrees of blur. Total occlusion requires caution because it removes visual input from the covered eye and makes the person functionally monocular.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: For adults with post-stroke eye-movement disorders, the guideline suggests treatment tailored to the particular disorder and referral to specialist eye services. While specialist care is pending, partial or total occlusion may relieve troublesome diplopia; total occlusion must be used cautiously because it eliminates input from the covered eye and renders the patient monocular. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: PICO 12: For adults with visual neglect due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: The question addresses visual neglect/inattention throughout the stroke pathway. Compensatory treatment aids adaptation, such as visual-scanning training; substitutive treatment uses a device or optical aid, such as prisms; restitutive treatment aims to restore visual attention.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: The critical outcomes were changes in neglect, daily activities and quality of life. There were 44 relevant comparative studies: 37 randomised trials, including cross-over trials, and seven cohort or cross-sectional studies. Median sample size was 30 (range 20–426; mean 51.0, SD 75.7). All reported daily-activity measures, and two also reported quality of life. Table 12.1 presents outcomes and GRADE assessments across intervention types; Figure 12 presents risk of bias. Heterogeneous interventions, outcomes and post-stroke timing prevented meta-analysis. Most studies had high risk of bias, including unblinded interpretation and limited completeness reporting. Investigated approaches included computerised, virtual-reality or cognitive training and eye patching; prism adaptation; robot-assisted training; brain stimulation; mirror therapy; visual-scanning or visuomotor training; and exercise. Individual studies combined or classified restorative, substitutive and compensatory components differently.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Study outcomes and treatment effects varied substantially. Prism adaptation and some visual-scanning approaches appeared promising for daily activities and quality of life. With computerised and robot-assisted training, both treatment and control groups sometimes improved without a significantly greater intervention effect. Mirror therapy and brain stimulation had variable effects on neglect measures but not on daily activities. Eye patching showed no significant change in neglect or daily-life measures. High-quality RCT evidence establishing improved daily activities is lacking; the effectiveness of neglect rehabilitation remains unproven, and current evidence neither supports nor rules out any rehabilitation approach.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: For adults with post-stroke visual neglect, the guideline suggests intervention tailored to the particular neglect syndrome and close collaboration among stroke teams, especially occupational therapy, neuropsychology and eye-care teams, including orthoptics and ophthalmology. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: PICO 13: For adults with other visual perceptual disorders due to stroke, does compensatory, substitute or restitutive intervention, compared to no intervention, improve activities and quality of daily life?
document_sections.content: The question covers visual-perceptual disorders at all stages of stroke care. Compensatory care helps adaptation, such as visual scanning or blinking; substitutive care uses an aid, such as a magnifier; restitutive care seeks to restore perception, such as through pharmacological treatment.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of current evidence
document_sections.content: Critical outcomes were visual perception, daily activities and quality of life. Four RCTs compared interventions with sham treatment; mean sample size was 32 (SD 8.5; median 30, range 24–44). Two investigated compensatory interventions and two investigated transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). All four reported visual-perception and daily-activity outcomes; one also reported quality of life. Table 13.1 gives intervention findings and GRADE assessments; Figure 13 gives risk-of-bias assessments. Differences in intervention, outcomes and treatment timing prevented meta-analysis. Most studies had high risk of bias, with heterogeneity, unblinded interpretation and limited reporting of complete or missing data.

document_sections.heading: Additional information
document_sections.content: Task training, including Nintendo games, has limited practicality in acute care but might help survivors in the chronic phase. Feasibility of early rTMS/tDCS warrants further study. Daily activities tended to improve with interventions, but improvement also occurred through control-group care or activities, so the source of benefit was uncertain. Evidence for quality-of-life change was insufficient. Research is constrained by heterogeneous perceptual disorders and too few people with any individual subtype to adequately power trials; sufficiently large studies require collaboration across recruitment sites. Clinicians should direct survivors to appropriate visual information and resources, including freely available materials.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-based Recommendation
document_sections.content: For adults with post-stroke visual-perceptual disorders, the guideline suggests an intervention tailored to the particular perceptual problem, provision of directions to visual information and resources, and close cooperation among stroke teams—especially occupational therapy—neuropsychology and eye-care teams, including orthoptics and ophthalmology. Quality of evidence: Very low ⊕. Strength of recommendation: Weak for intervention ↑?

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The guideline uses GRADE to support decisions about stroke-related visual impairment. Table 14 and Figure 14 bring together its recommendations and expert-consensus statements. Visual problems affect about 75% of stroke survivors by reported prevalence and about 60% by reported incidence. Rowe and colleagues identified impaired central acuity in 56%, eye-movement abnormalities in 40%, field loss in 28%, visual inattention in 27% and perceptual disorders in 5%. Assessment and care are unequal; females, people of black ethnicity, those with lower socioeconomic status or educational attainment, and older people are described as particularly disadvantaged. Stroke may disrupt interpretation and integration of sensory input; an estimated 70% of perceived sensory information is visual. Visual impairment is negatively associated with rehabilitation and quality of life and can affect mobility, navigation, interaction, self-care, independence, mood and driving. Screening should therefore cover acuity, fields, neglect and eye movements so that a survivor whose impairment breaches applicable driving rules is not discharged without driving-related information; requirements vary between countries, and follow-up should reassess visual requirements. Treating diplopia with prisms or a patch may restore visual function needed for driving. No standardised stroke-vision detection protocol currently exists. Variation in screening, specialist referral, treatment, information and communication adapted to visual impairment contributes to unmet need, inequity and poorer patient experience. Norup et al. identified visual problems in 24% at initial neurological examination; some who declined further assessment said they had not noticed a problem. Among survivors with neglect, unawareness of visuospatial deficits predicted poorer daily functioning more strongly than deficit severity or time since stroke. An estimated 40–60% with new visual impairment do not or cannot report symptoms; some remain unaware despite caregivers observing collisions or accidents. Missed deficits may mean missed rehabilitation, and unrecognised field loss may create road-safety risks.

document_sections.heading: Table 14. Vision guideline recommendations and expert consensus statements.
document_sections.content: The table consolidates diagnosis and treatment guidance. PICO 1 suggests screening adults after stroke with a validated tool or specialist eye assessment to improve visual-problem detection; specialist assessment further improves diagnostic accuracy. Quality of evidence: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias. Strength: Weak for intervention ↑?. For PICO 2, evidence is insufficient to recommend early screening on an evidence basis: Low ⊕⊕; Not assessable (–). Nevertheless, 10 of 10 experts advise screening within 3–4days when feasible, with most assessed within 1week, using specialist assessment or at least a validated tool. For PICO 3, PICO 4, PICO 5 and PICO 6, evidence is insufficient for an evidence-based comparison of targeted screening or specialist assessment with routine stroke screening: QUADAS-2 Medium risk of bias; Not assessable (–). For each condition—field loss, central impairment, eye-movement disorders and perceptual disorders—10 of 10 experts support early screening, feasible within 3–4days for many and within 1week for most, using specialist assessment or at least a validated tool. Their statements say screening detects more affected people than routine stroke screening and specialist assessment increases accuracy. PICO 7 suggests screening for neglect, with specialist assessment and a test battery to improve detection accuracy: QUADAS-2 High risk of bias; Weak for intervention ↑?. PICO 8 suggests compensatory scanning/search for field loss and early treatment when feasible and acceptable. PICO 9 suggests thrombolysis for ocular stroke within 4.5h: Very low ⊕; Weak for intervention ↑?. PICO 10 finds insufficient evidence for an evidence-based intervention recommendation: Very low ⊕; Not assessable (–); 10 of 10 experts nevertheless favour prompt acuity management, prescribed and updated spectacles, information and aids. PICO 11 suggests tailored eye-movement management, specialist referral and cautious partial or total occlusion for troublesome diplopia while awaiting care: Very low ⊕; Weak for intervention ↑?. PICO 12 suggests individualised neglect care and multidisciplinary collaboration. PICO 13 suggests tailored perceptual care, information and multidisciplinary collaboration: Very low ⊕; Weak for intervention ↑?.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Clinicians use differing visual and perceptual assessment tools, with varying validation and normative support; tools used in practice may not appear in published studies. Reliable screening methods require development, evaluation and validation to enable early rehabilitation. Despite limited high-quality research, early screening is consistently described as feasible, acceptable and better at detecting visual impairment, with potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, referral and rehabilitation access. Ideally, an eye-team member assesses every survivor on the stroke unit to enable prompt diagnosis and management. Where specialist access is limited, the guideline recommends validated tools usable by any stroke-team member. Prehospital and emergency checklists supplement FAST or NIHSS and take less than 5min; they assist stroke recognition, particularly posterior-circulation stroke. More detailed inpatient bedside tools take between 10 and 30min, assess several visual functions, and can be used with survivors who have communication or mild cognitive difficulties. Screening is feasible within 3–4days of onset. Anyone initially unable to participate should be offered it later when able. Standard stroke checklists do not adequately test acuity, all gaze positions, field defects beyond hemianopia or perceptual disorders beyond neglect. No single test reliably excludes neglect: multiple tests should be attempted. The guideline supports adding one or more of line bisection, figure copying and baking tray task to a cancellation test, in line with The European Academy of Neurology, and notes its recommendation of the Catherine Beregeo Scale for functional assessment. Cognitive or communication impairment should not automatically prevent screening: hand signals and alternative specialist techniques can permit assessment.

document_sections.heading: Figure 14. Summary recommendations. A: Diagnosis.
document_sections.content: The diagnostic pathway places rapid BEFAST, PreHAST or V-FAST checks in prehospital and emergency settings, followed by standardised, validated screening on acute stroke units within 3-4 days of onset and in rehabilitation or community care. Rapid checklists take <5min and assist stroke-detection decisions as additions to FAST, or to FAST and NIHSS in emergency care. An eye-team assessment for every survivor is preferred when available because it permits rapid accurate diagnosis and early management. Otherwise, a stroke-team member can use a standardised validated tool taking <30min to screen major post-stroke visual impairments, repeat assessment and triage referrals.

document_sections.heading: Figure 14. Summary recommendations. B: Management.
document_sections.content: The management pathway includes prompt acuity measures such as glasses for central impairment; tailored care and partial or total occlusion for troublesome diplopia in eye-movement disorders; compensatory scanning/search for homonymous field loss; thrombolysis for central retinal artery occlusion within 4.5 hours unless contraindicated; and tailored care for neglect or perceptual disorders. Management should begin as soon as possible, within days of onset, to maximise remaining vision and participation in rehabilitation. Collaboration among stroke, neuropsychology and eye-care teams is encouraged, alongside condition-specific information, resources and aids.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: When visual impairment is the sole presenting stroke sign, recognising stroke as its cause allows immediate stroke-unit referral and may enable reperfusion within its therapeutic window. No factors predict complete, partial or absent visual recovery. Accurate spectacles, prisms, coping strategies and magnification may help while recovery remains uncertain. Rehabilitation evidence differs by impairment. For central retinal artery occlusion, timely thrombolysis within 4.5h may improve visual function, especially acuity, and requires coordination across stroke, neurology, ophthalmology and primary care. For field loss, compensatory scanning/search has the clearest indication of benefit for daily activities, and early treatment supports adaptation. Although stroke-specific studies of reduced acuity and eye-movement disorders are limited, relevant intervention research exists in other acquired brain injuries; eye-care specialist involvement helps apply it. Evidence for neglect and perceptual-disorder treatments remains limited, requiring further research and neuropsychology collaboration. Needed research includes adequately powered diagnostic-accuracy studies and RCTs, cost-effectiveness evaluation, core outcomes combining objective and subjective visual measures with daily activities and quality of life, appropriate follow-up, and assessment of early vision testing and hospital stay. Further work should examine sensitivity and discrimination awareness within field loss, falls and driving. The recommendations represent currently available evidence and may be revised when further scientific data emerge.
